newsitem.title: USA: High court rejection of Ohio muni case welcomed.
newsitem.headline: High court rejection of Ohio muni case welcomed.

text.p: Municipal bond market participants breathed a sigh of relief Monday that the U.S. Supreme Court had once again declined to hear a challenge to a state's taxation of income on out-of-state municipal bonds.
"I think basically it's a vote for the status quo," said Richard Lehmann, president of Bond Investors Association. "It's a can of worms the U.S. Supreme court decided not to open up."
He added that outlawing the practice would be "terribly unsettling for the whole municipal bond industry."

Richard Ciccarone, a senior vice president at Van Kampen American Capital, agreed that the elimination of double tax-exemption "would cause havoc in the financial markets." He said the high court may have taken note that the practice has been in place for a while and the court's decision not to hear the case was a reflection of the strengthening of states' rights.
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday declined to hear the case brought by Cleveland area bondholder Serene Shaper against the Ohio Department of Revenue.

The court's refusal marked the second time the high court has declined to take up the case. In October 1995, the court passed on the first part of the case which sought a declaratory judgment that Ohio's in-state tax exemption on municipal bonds was unconstitutional.

The second part of the case sought a refund of $6,000 in Ohio income taxes Shaper paid between 1988 and 1991 on interest earned from her out-of-state municipal bonds. The refund had been rejected by the Ohio revenue department, the state tax appeals board and finally by the Ohio Supreme Court last August.

While a spokesman for the Ohio Attorney General's Office, which defended the state's revenue department in the lawsuit, called the matter closed, Clint Krislov, Shaper's Chicago attorney, said he would continue to find a way to force the nation's high court to hear the case.

Shaper's petition to the U.S. Supreme Court argued that the issue of whether a state could under the commerce clause of the U.S. Constitution "discriminatorily impose" its income tax on other states' municipal bonds "is an issue of overwhelming timeliness and importance."
The petition stated that 37 states besides Ohio tax income on out-of-state municipals.
Lehmann said he agreed the practice was "inherently unconstitutional."

"I don't think a state should be allowed to discriminate against products of other states," he said. "I guess when it comes to securities, the supreme court decided it didn't want to get into that issue."

The case troubled municipal market participants, including the state of Minnesota, which enacted a law in 1995 that outlined its intention to prospectively tax interest on in-state municipals should the U.S. Supreme Court rule in-state tax exemptions unconstitutional.
